::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A proposed study
This page describes a **research proposal** (June 2026). Data access and ethics approval are still to come, so it sets out the question, design and hypotheses. It contains no results.
:::

## The problem

We usually assume that people in cities have better access to care, and therefore better health outcomes, than people in rural areas. In Nairobi's informal settlements, such as **Kibera, Mathare, Korogocho, Viwandani and Mukuru**, that assumption breaks down for maternal health.

Kenya's maternal mortality estimates rely mostly on facility reports in the **Kenya Health Information System (KHIS)**. But many deaths in these settlements happen at home, in transit, or in unregistered clinics, so they never reach a facility register. Recorded rates can therefore look *lowest* where the true burden may be *highest*. If resources follow recorded deaths, they go to the wrong places.

The size of this undercount, and *where* it is concentrated, is unknown. This project sets out to measure it rather than assume it.

## Research questions

1. Do ward-level KHIS maternal death counts show **more variation and more zeros** than a standard Poisson model would predict?
2. Which ward-level factors best predict whether a maternal death is **actually captured** in KHIS?
3. Once missed deaths are accounted for, what is the **estimated true maternal mortality** in each ward, and which socioeconomic factors are most strongly linked to the gap?

## The model

The core idea is to separate two processes that together produce the number we see in KHIS: how many women **actually die**, and how many of those deaths the health system **detects**.

```{=html}
<div class="model-diagram" role="img" aria-label="Diagram: a mortality layer (ward poverty, home birth rate) determines true maternal deaths; a detection layer (facility density, community health worker coverage, KHIS reporting completeness) determines how many of those become recorded KHIS deaths.">
  <div class="md-layer md-mort"><span class="md-label">Mortality layer</span><ul><li>Ward poverty level</li><li>Home birth rate</li></ul></div>
  <div class="md-arrow md-a1">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="md-node md-true"><strong>True maternal deaths</strong><span class="md-sub">unobserved</span></div>
  <div class="md-arrow md-a2">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="md-node md-out"><strong>Recorded KHIS deaths</strong><span class="md-sub">what we see</span></div>
  <div class="md-arrow md-up">&uarr;</div>
  <div class="md-layer md-detect"><span class="md-label">Detection layer</span><ul><li>Facility density</li><li>Community health worker coverage</li><li>KHIS reporting completeness</li></ul></div>
</div>
```

[The recorded count is shaped by both how many women actually die and how many of those deaths the health system detects.]{.md-caption}

- **Excess zeros and overdispersion:** a **zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB)** model separates wards with genuinely no deaths from wards where deaths simply went unrecorded.
- **Detection:** a logistic component models the probability that deaths are missed, as a function of facility density, community health worker coverage and reporting completeness.
- **Calibration:** independent **verbal autopsy data** from the Nairobi Urban Health and Demographic Surveillance System (NUHDSS) in Korogocho and Viwandani, run by the African Population and Health Research Center, act as the reference for calibrating detection.
- **Spatial smoothing:** a **BYM2** random effect lets neighbouring wards inform each other's estimates, separating spatially structured from unstructured variation.
- **Output:** posterior estimates with **95% credible intervals** of the true number of maternal deaths in each of Nairobi's 85 wards, mapped as a "shadow mortality" burden.
- **Tools:** fitted in **R-INLA**, which is fast and well suited to spatial disease mapping.

## Data sources

| Source | What it provides |
|---|---|
| Kenya Health Information System (Ministry of Health) | Ward-level maternal death counts and reporting completeness |
| NUHDSS (African Population and Health Research Center) | Aggregated verbal autopsy maternal deaths, Korogocho and Viwandani |
| Kenya Master Health Facility List | Facility locations and density |
| Nairobi County Health Department | Community Health Unit coverage |
| 2019 Census and 2022 Kenya DHS | Ward socioeconomic profiles and birth-rate estimates |
| WorldPop | Age- and sex-specific population estimates |

## What sets it apart

To my knowledge, no previous study has modelled maternal mortality **within a single city at ward level**, or used an **independent verbal-autopsy reference to model the detection process** itself. The goal is a practical tool that shows health officials *where the system is failing to see deaths*, not only where deaths are recorded.

## Hypotheses

- Recorded counts will show substantial overdispersion and zero-inflation.
- Detection will depend measurably on health-system capacity.
- Estimated true mortality will most exceed recorded figures in the least-served settlements, with poverty and home births as key drivers. If so, part of the "urban advantage" in maternal health is an artefact of incomplete measurement.

::: {.privacy-note}
<i class="bi bi-shield-check"></i> Ethics approval will be sought from the USIU-Africa review committee and NACOSTI. Formal data use agreements will govern access to KHIS, NUHDSS and community health data, including secure storage and a ban on re-identification. Findings will be shared with the Nairobi County Health Management Team and APHRC before public release.
:::
